utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know these persons. I didn't know their ranks or anything, but I think he had two junior officers of the VRS as his escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any other VRS soldiers in the centre of Zepa at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I left around midday on the 26th of July, I don't recall any other VRS soldiers being there, and I can't say anything about their presence afterwards because I had left by that time for Boksanica. But up until midday on the 26th of July, I don't recall having seen any VRS soldiers in the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That will do fine for my purposes. Therefore the only people who could have mistreated the evacuees, remembering Mr. Thayer's question, was General Tolimir or these two junior officers. There was no one else from the VRS there up to the point that you left; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone else being there, but let me just note that the mistreatment could have occurred at other places, not just in Zepa. In Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Rogatica along the way. So what I mean when I say that there was no mistreatment, I was -- I'm referring to the whole process in Zepa from the time when they were put on the buses in Zepa and until their arrival at the final destination in Kladanj when they got off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Continuing to paint the picture, were the Ukrainian battalion representatives present during the evacuation period prior to your departure from the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but now as to their number and as to what they did I can't really tell you, but they were there because most of the UNPROFOR soldiers had come to the UNPROFOR base in Zepa from their various check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any armed Muslim men in the centre of Zepa at that point?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any one of those people who had come there to say good-bye to their families had been armed. I really can't tell you. Perhaps somebody may have carried a pistol or something like that, but I didn't see any rifles or any such weapons on those people who had come to say good-bye to their wives and children. I didn't see any weapons on them, and it is not quite logical at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know where the bulk of Colonel Palic's brigade were at that point?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were at the Zepska-Planina, the Zepa mountain, which is a mountain to the north of the centre of Zepa. Q. I'm asking you that question because in your witness statement - and if need be I could show it to you - but for the benefit of others it's at page 8 towards the bottom of the page in English. You said: "On the 26th July, the military-aged personnel from Zepa withdrew to the mountains, and that day around noon I went to the check-point at Boksanica, and I exchanged myself for Tolimir, complying with Mladic's request." Firstly, is that sentence from your statement? And perhaps I should say for the benefit of the record that's a statement dated the 19th of January of 1998. Is that sentence from your statement correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at a later stage I realised that this sentence has been mistranslated and that it does not really correspond to the state of affairs, and I have already pointed out that the real -- the whole truth is what I now stated in my evidence regarding my presence at check-point number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's my fault, Witness, but it's really the date that I'm particularly interested in. You say there that on the 26th of July the military-aged personnel from Zepa withdrew to the mountains. Two questions, and I'll ask them together if I may. The first is is that correct? And if it is correct, where were they on the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was occupied by with completely -- with other things in that period. This thing that I put in here is based on the things that I heard from others. On the 25th of July, this is the date when the hostilities or when armed combat ceased in and around the Zepa enclave, the morning of the 25th. So it follows that all those who were of military age and who had weapons, they first went to see their families to organise things and to say good-bye, to see their wives and their children, because at that time an arrangement had already been made, or an agreement had already been made that they should be evacuated on buses. But generally speaking, it was, I don't know, the 26th. I assume that by that time most of them were already at the Zepa mountain. I don't know what's incorrect here in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One last question in relation to this area. You've told us that General Tolimir was there with two of his junior officers. You were there till midday on the 26th of July. Who was guaranteeing General Tolimir's safety for the first 24 hours or so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was as follows: General Tolimir arrived with the representative of the International Red Cross, that was on the 25th. The UNPROFOR soldiers or some of their officers, and as far as I know throughout this time he was escorted by Colonel Avdo Palic. And in the evening of the 25th, General Tolimir left Zepa on a convoy and came back that morning maybe an hour or two hours before I left for check-point number 2 where I was to guarantee his safety. So this is how it all developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've just mentioned the International Red Cross. It's right that you recall representatives from the ICRC arriving in Zepa on the 25th of July to monitor the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I remember that this was a team, three staff members of the International Red Cross. So I can confirm that on the first day they were there. The next day I left for Boksanica. So I don't know whether they monitored the remainder of the evacuation. But on the first day, the 25th, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to change the subject, please, and return to the beginning of your evidence. Am I right in saying that you moved to Zepa in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you moved there did you have any relatives who lived there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I lived as a refugee in a house of a local resident - but he was not a relative of mine or anything like that - because I didn't have anywhere else to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there anyone in Zepa, to the best of your knowledge, who had the same name as you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first name, yes, I guess. There must have been other (redacted). At least one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I meant to -- perhaps I should have been clear. I meant your first name with your surname. I think you've answered the question by saying no to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody had the same first and last name. There was a relative of mine, but he was not in Zepa during the war, and -- but his -- he -- so he was not in Zepa. He was in Sarajevo, and his name is also (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's redact as well, please. Please, Witness, I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You must be feeling -- or start feeling tired now, because everyone else is, but let's try to work a little bit less. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For obvious reasons the other members of our team are about five minutes ahead of me. They have somewhat of an advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, in your evidence and in the witness statement that I have already referred to, you make no mention of having done any army service. Was that because you weren't asked, or was it for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first period when the military activities started my mother was sick, and I did not do the national service in the former JNA, so that I spent this initial period taking care of my mother. So I was not serving in the army in any capacity at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you in the army at all at any stage during the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell it us about the improper way, then, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, socialising with these people and Colonel Avdo Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you part of Colonel Palic's brigade in any sense at all as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to tell you. Not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you carry or use a gun or any other weapon during the period either before or after the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any official role, specific task in Colonel Palic's brigade assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that at the beginning Colonel Palic had some radio stations, and because I am an electrical engineer he had me look at them. So that may have been a period of 15 or 20 days before we were forced to leave the place where we lived at the time. I went to Zeleni Jadar then, and I returned, as I indicated at the beginning. I returned to Zepa in early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why do you mention that now?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please clarify your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying that you performed some role in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question was whether I did anything or had any contacts, and that is my response. Avdo called me at one point regarding some radio stations. I had a look at them, but that was it. That was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it was not official as far as you were concerned? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- yes -- no. It was not official.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two things before we have the break. One is the following: You know that there is pending a decision that we need to hand down on the remaining -- no. The witness can be escorted out. He doesn't have to listen. Yes. About the three remaining witnesses from the list of 12 that the Prosecution asked or sought to have converted into 92 ter witnesses. Now, we've been going through this amongst ourselves, and the conclusion that we come to is that it's difficult for us to decide one way or another unless we have at our disposal the proposed 92 ter statements. As soon as we have those available and we find the time to go through them, we will be in a position to hand down our decision. Since the first of these witnesses is expected to start testifying pretty soon, I would suggest that these be handed at the earliest possible. The other thing is the following: Yesterday, I asked you to possibly come back this morning with your response in relation to the Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness number 135. Are there any objections from any of the Defence teams for the protective measures sought, which are pseudonym and facial distortion? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we with grant the motion here and now without much formality. It's being granted already. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Following on from my questions before the break, could we now look at 6D83, please. Whilst this is being put up on the screen, I can say that this is a document dated the 2nd of February of 1994. It's signed by Avdo Palic from the 1st Zepa Light Brigade, and it's to the 1st Corps of the armed forces of Sarajevo. It's quite a long document which deals with the organisation of the brigade and to some extent its history. And I would like to ask you, first of all, Witness, if you could have a look at the third page in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast, please. Sorry, I should have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Middle of that third page, fourth page in English, it says: "On 18 October 1992, Avdo Palic was appointed commander of the Zepa region armed forces." I'm going to summarise here: Names a deputy, names someone as an assistant commander, then names an individual called Hasanovic for intelligence and security, and then it names someone as chief of communications. That's your name, isn't it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name, and that tallies with what I previously said, but no particular activities are mentioned. This document is not familiar to me. It was drafted in 1994, as you said, and this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the passage just above the one I have referred to on the same page. It describes there the fact that two detachments called 4 Juni, and I quote, "were formed." It talks about the 2nd Zepa Detachment, names again Mr. Palic as the commander, and has you as the chief of communications. This suggests, does it not, that you were part of Commander Palic's armed formation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the conclusion one might draw from this document, that the actual state of affairs was such as I have already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then if we scroll down, we see that on the 27th of January of 1993, the actual 1st Zepa Brigade was formed from the two detachments, and again you're there as chief of communications. This is making it clear that you were part of the brigade and its activities. You weren't there in some unofficial position as you are trying to suggest. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this document, and as I have already said, the actual state of affairs was as I have described it, but this document seems to indicate that I was present over there and involved in certain activities. But let me repeat this. At the time it I wasn't even in Zepa. I was mostly in Zeleni Jadar looking for food. That was the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll ask you one other thing about this document. Could you have a look at the very top of page 3, please. This is page 3 in the English, at the bottom of the page. And we see the description of the 1st detachment and the units that were formed, and we see that a Cavcici company had been formed and it gives the name of the commander. I'm not going to read the name. You can read it, and perhaps you can read it to yourself. How many people with that name did you know in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find that. I don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I want you to have the one in your own language. It's the fourth line down at the top of page 3. That's the entry I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a name there begins with a letter "D" second name has a letter "M" on it. As I say, let's not read it out, please, but how many people did you know with that name in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think just one person. I didn't know those people very well, but on the whole, just one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did that person have any connection with the army, the police, or both? When I say the army, I mean the brigade, the SJB, or both?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the person concerned was in the police force, performed certain duties within the civilian police. When I arrived in spring and got to know those people a little better, well, up until that point in time I hadn't been in Zepa at all, and I practically knew no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That leads me on conveniently to the relationship in Zepa in really 1993, 1994, and 1995 between the police and the army. We know that there was ill feeling between Mr. Sahic and Mr. Palic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was a personal disagreement. We could put it that way. Or perhaps something worse, and that's in fact related to that period of time in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You shared a building with them, namely the farm cooperative building in the centre of Zepa. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a point of clarification. We've been talking about both Commander Palic and this other individual, Mr. Sahic. So I just wanted to clarify, when you say when you were with them, were you referring to the army and the police, in the same building? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The army namely the brigade and the police namely the SJB, and the municipal authorities, in a fewer part, shared the same building in the centre of Zepa. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there is something that should be explained. The Executive Board was located there. I think they were on the first floor, in the basement -- or, rather on the ground floor the civilian police had its premises, and for a while Colonel Avdo Palic had his office on one of the floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did Colonel Palic have his office on one of the floors?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was the second half of 1993 and in 1994. I really can't remember all the details, but I think it was in the second half of 1993 and in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you were there. You knew both of these individuals, Colonel Palic, Mr. Sahic. Tell the Trial Chamber what their dispute was all about, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there and got to know those people -- but I should point out that I had met Mr. Palic a lot earlier, and it was only then that I met Mr. Sahic. The way I saw things is that in psychological terms, they had very similar personalities. Everyone thought he should be the number one person. Everyone thought he should be in charge, and that's what gave rise to misunderstandings, and perhaps at a certain point in time misunderstandings arose with regard to the sharing of responsibility. The question was whether the police should be under the control of the army or not. I think that was the main reason for this misunderstanding or disagreement between Avdo Palic and the chief of police, Hurem Sahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the division of resources between the police and the army? By resources I mean money. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What money do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Deutschmarks, Witness. That's what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, German marks, but from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You tell us. As far as you were aware, was Colonel Palic enriching either himself or his brigade at the expense of everyone else in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least as far as I know, no one was enriching himself. The money you have in mind was sent from Sarajevo, I believe, according to the information I have. This was done on one occasion in 1993. And as to whether it was done again in 1994, I don't know. I really don't know how much money was sent, but I do know that the money was distributed to army members, but it was so long ago that I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's see if I can help jog your memory and show you 6049, a document that's already in evidence. This is a series of documents, all of which come from Mr. Sahic and are basically a collection of remarks, or perhaps complaints, that he sent to various high officials within the BiH organisation collectively, and I'd like you to have a look, please, at page 2 in your language. Page 2 in the English as well. And if you could go to the bottom of the page, please. I'm not going to read this out because it's already in evidence, but I'd like you to read it to yourself from the word Jedani [phoen], which basically the various forms of disinformation spread by the people. If you could read that to yourself to the end of that paragraph. I beg your pardon. My fault entirely. Sorry, Witness. Well, I -- I've shown you that passage, so let's deal with it now. This is at page 3 in the English. I do apologise to the Court and to you, Witness. This is a passage that deals with a proposal for what is called in inverted commas, "The autonomy of Zepa." This was sometime in late 1994. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. It's the first time I've heard about a document and seen such a document. When I was in Zepa, I had no information about what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of discussions along those lines by Colonel Palic. That's your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have absolutely no knowledge. This is the first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you that anyway, so let's go back to the point that I was at a moment ago. Towards the top of the second page, same page, the paragraph that starts "Razne dezinformacije." Could you read that to paragraph yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that is the passage I alluded to earlier, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it true, Witness, that the 1st Zepa Brigade received 400.000 Deutschmarks and kept it to themselves?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this amount since I don't know anything about it, but I said that I did know there were resources that were sent to the Zepa Brigade. As for the way in which it was spent, as for the amounts concerned, I didn't know anything about that, so I can't confirm anything with regard to the amount itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did your Executive Committee receive any of that money?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't, no. As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's one other part of this document I'd like to ask you about. It's the next page in the B/C/S where we see numeral 1. In the English it's on the third page. And I am going to read this out. It says: "In October 1993, on his way back from Sarajevo as a member of the Zepa delegation, the commander of the aforementioned brigade stole 5.000 Deutschmarks from the money which he was bringing to the Zepa RP." You were with him on that journey to and from Sarajevo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was towards the end of September, and we returned at the beginning of October. As for the amount of 5.000 marks, well, I can't confirm whom he received that from, whether he received it, how he spent it. I really have no such information, but we were in Sarajevo together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea on what basis Mr. Sahic made that very serious allegation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the result of the misunderstandings between Mr. Sahic and Colonel Avdo Palic, and as a result this document was drafted which he sent to Sarajevo. As to all the details that Mr. Sahic has referred to, I haven't got any precise information. So I know that some money was received, but as to whether anything was stolen, I can't confirm that. That wasn't my field of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As one of the senior municipal representatives in the enclave, did you try to keep the peace between the military and police leaders?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When pursuing my duties, I had -- I was on good terms with Mr. Sahic and with Colonel Avdo Palic. Could this be described as reconciling people? Perhaps in certain situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic, if I may, and that's this: Was there any attempt by the authorities - and for this purpose again I mean either the police or army or civil authorities - to stop the local population leaving the enclave should they choose to do so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any particular activities in that area. There were attempts to leave the enclave, the Zepa enclave. These duties were police duties, and given the time that has passed, well, I know there were some stories, but I can't remember all the details. According to the decision of duties, this should have been the police's responsibility, but as to what activities they were involved in, as to what was done in that area, I really can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any problem with people who wanted to leave departing?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that? Which problems? What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did it concern you? Personally.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that some wounded and sick people tried to find a way of getting out of Zepa. As far as being concerned goes, again given all the time that has passed it's difficult for me to go into any details. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why in the answer you've just given did you specify wounded and sick people?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant just the sick, because I remember that some people tried to find a way to move out, those who got sick in 1993 or 1994 and who had serious health problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm talking about able-bodied people who wanted to leave. And let me make it clear I mean civilians who wanted to leave. Did it concern you that these people wanted to leave, and were you part of any attempt to stop them leaving?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people could go to Srebrenica, to the Srebrenica area, without any problems if you could say that, but further afield the whole territory was controlled by the Republika Srpska army, and you could not go there. But this whole story about people leaving Zepa, I don't really understand fully what you're driving at. In fact, everybody as a rule wanted to get out of Zepa, but there was no way that this could be done. It just couldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D39, please. This is a document from Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic, dated the 26th of May, 1995, to Colonel Palic, and it says: "In order to prevent certain civilians and any members of the BH army from leaving the territory of Zepa without permission and illegally, it will be necessary to exercise the following measures." And then the first dash it basically says cooperation with the SJB, a plan to prevent people from leaving. Second dash, and I quote again: "In addition to guarding certain routes and areas, it will be necessary to conduct political work among the Zepa's town people and soldiers pointing out the danger of leaving the area. For this purpose, engage the assistance for morale, the imam and all prominent people who could have an influence on anyone from Zepa intending to leave the area." Firstly, Witness, would you accept that you were one of the prominent people in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know what General Enver meant when he said prominent people. This is, I believe, the first time that I see this document, and the leaving of Zepa is here described in way that would suggest that all it took was to get on a bus, scheduled bus service, and just leave. This whole idea is quite unclear to me, because how could one leave Zepa? There was just no way to do it except if you wanted to go to the Srebrenica area. And that is why this order that relates to people leaving Zepa is in fact a little bit exaggerated. The wording is a bit exaggerated. I can confirm that perhaps a dozen or so members of the army managed to cross through the territory of -- held by the Republika Srpska army and into the territory held by the BH army, but this was very risky, and I don't think that this instruction -- I don't know whether this instruction actually refers to this incident, but at any rate, it sounds as if one could just get on a bus and leave Zepa, and that was just not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So Hadzihasanovic's order or instruction never filtered down to you in any way at all. You knew nothing about this. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just see this instruction. He suggested that 285th Brigade -- I don't think -- I don't recall knowing anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally on this, as far as you were concerned, it was not an issue that any of the authorities in Zepa was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to clarify your question, because I just don't understand the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on if I may. Earlier today you were asked by Mr. Thayer, at page 3, line 7, as to whether you were aware of arms and ammunition reaching the enclave despite the demilitarisation agreement, and this was your answer and I quote: "According to the information I had in the second half of 1994, weapons were delivered by helicopter, as well as ammunition."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You -- am I right to infer from that answer that you know nothing about deliveries of weapons in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. The helicopter deliveries went on in the second half of 1994 and in early 1995. So that was a period that actually covered those two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell the Trial Chamber about 1995 when Mr. Thayer asked you that question?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps it's simply a matter of my answer not being precise enough. But there is no problem, and this is not at issue at all. It was the second half of 1994 and 1995. I assume that I was just not precise enough in the answer that I gave you -- that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the time as a municipal leader, how did you view this illegal arms supply in clear breach of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not something that I was supposed to deal with or that I had any control or influence over in accordance with the distribution of tasks that we had. This was something that the army was in charge of, and all the information that I gave are -- that's the information that I learned from others. I never had any documents or any papers about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let me help you a bit. Did you view it as the road to disaster in the sense that in due course armed hostilities were bound to follow from this arming?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fate of Zepa was something that had to be resolved in some way. The situation as it was was not something that could continue endlessly. I don't remember what my views were of this matter, but at any rate this is something that everybody was worried about, how we could get out of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And is it right to assume, Witness, that you knew full well that those arms that were being supplied to Palic and his men were being used for sabotage operation by Palic and his men on Serbs outside the enclave throughout 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about one such military action in 1995. Now, as for any such actions in 1994 or from May 1993 onwards, I don't remember, and I don't think that there were any. But I can confirm that there was one such action in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think my last question for the day: The one in 1995 was when and where, please? The one that you knew about.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all as to when it happened, it was in mid-June 1995. I don't know about the details of the action. And I think it was carried out in the north-eastern part of the enclave, but I really don't know what the objective of the action was and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If that's a convenient moment for Your Honour. I will have to conclude there for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Witness, we'll continue on Monday, Monday morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. In the meantime may I just repeat what I had told you yesterday, namely that you are not to contact or allow anyone to contact you and discuss matters related to your testimony. So have a nice weekend, everybody, and please, we'll meet again on Monday morning.
